title: Encoding and Decoding a List of Strings

concept: Design an algorithm to encode a list of strings into a single string and decode it back to the original list. The encode and decode methods must be stateless and handle any valid string content including special characters, empty strings, and delimiters.

solutions.label: Escape Character Delimiter
solutions.summary: Use a delimiter to separate strings, and an escape character to handle cases where the delimiter appears within the strings themselves.

solutions.label: Length-Prefixed Encoding
solutions.summary: Prefix each string with its length followed by a fixed separator character, allowing unambiguous decoding without escaping.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["List of Strings"]:::red --> B["encode()"]:::red
    B --> C["Single String"]:::red
    C --> D["decode()"]:::red
    D --> E["Original List of Strings"]:::red
    classDef red fill:#f87171,stroke:#dc2626,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. I'd like you to design two functions: encode and decode. The encode function takes a list of strings and converts it into a single string. The decode function takes that single string and converts it back into the original list. The key constraint is that these functions must be stateless.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Interesting. So I need to make sure the round trip is lossless. Can the input strings contain any characters, including special characters, numbers, or even empty strings?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the strings can contain any valid character, including symbols, spaces, and empty strings. The list itself can also be empty.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So the tricky part is choosing a way to separate strings that won't conflict with the string content. If I just use a comma, a string containing a comma would break the decoding. Let me think about approaches that handle this cleanly.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. That's the core challenge. How do you guarantee that your separator or encoding scheme is unambiguous regardless of the input content?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Right. Let me summarize: I need encode and decode functions that handle any string content, including empty strings, special characters, and delimiters. The functions must be stateless. I'll start with a simpler approach and then optimize.

sections.title: Escape Character Delimiter
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Input: ['ab','a#b']"]:::blue --> B["Choose '#' as delimiter"]:::blue
    B --> C["Escape existing '#' in strings"]:::blue
    C --> D["'ab' stays 'ab'"]:::blue
    C --> E["'a#b' becomes 'a##b'"]:::blue
    D --> F["Join with '/#'"]:::blue
    E --> F
    F --> G["Encoded: 'ab/#a##b'"]:::blue
    G --> H["Decode: split on '/# ' and unescape '##'"]:::blue
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#2563eb,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is to use a delimiter approach with escape characters. I'll pick a delimiter, say the hash symbol, and an escape character, say the slash. Before joining, I escape any existing hash or slash characters within each string. Then I join strings with a unique delimiter like slash-hash.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That could work. Can you walk through how decoding handles the escaped characters?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: During decoding, I scan the encoded string. When I see slash-hash, I know it's a real delimiter between strings. When I see double-hash or double-slash, I know those are escaped characters within a string. I convert them back to single characters.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What about the time and space complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Both are O of n times k, where n is the number of strings and k is the average length. We scan every character during both encoding and decoding. The downside is the implementation is tricky. We need careful character-by-character parsing during decode, and bugs can easily creep in with nested escaping.

sections.title: Length-Prefixed Encoding
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Input: ['hello','world','']"]:::orange --> B["Encode each string"]:::orange
    B --> C["'5#hello'"]:::orange
    B --> D["'5#world'"]:::orange
    B --> E["'0#'"]:::orange
    C --> F["Combined: '5#hello5#world0#'"]:::orange
    D --> F
    E --> F
    F --> G["Decode: read length, skip '#', extract substring"]:::orange
    G --> H["Output: ['hello','world','']"]:::orange
    classDef orange fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: A much cleaner approach is length-prefixed encoding. For each string, I prepend its length followed by a hash symbol. For example, hello becomes five-hash-hello. The hash is just a fixed separator between the length and the content.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Why is this better than the escape character approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is that we never need to escape anything. Since we know the exact length of each string, we simply read that many characters after the separator. Even if the string content contains digits or hash symbols, it doesn't matter because we already know where the string ends.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How does decoding work step by step?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: During decoding, I maintain a pointer. I find the next hash symbol, parse everything before it as the length, then extract that many characters after the hash as the string. I advance the pointer past those characters and repeat. For empty strings, the length is zero, so I just read zero characters and get an empty string back.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time complexity is O of n times k, same as before. Space complexity is also O of n times k for the encoded string. But this approach is far simpler to implement, less error-prone, and handles all edge cases naturally without special escaping logic.

    classDef orange fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great work. Both approaches have the same time complexity, but the length-prefixed encoding is clearly the better design. What's the main takeaway from this problem?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key lesson is that when designing serialization formats, including metadata like the length of each element makes parsing unambiguous. Instead of fighting with escape characters and edge cases, we let the length tell us exactly where each string starts and ends. It's a pattern used in real protocols like HTTP and binary formats.
